questions.title: A cargo box that may slide or tip
questions.subtopic: A cargo box that may slide or tip
questions.stem:
A rigid box of mass $6.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ has a rectangular cross section $0.80\,\mathrm m$ by $0.40\,\mathrm m$ and its centre of mass at the geometric centre. The horizontal floor has $\mu_s=0.50$ and $\mu_k=0.30$. Use $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

First the box rests on its $0.80\,\mathrm m$ wide base. A horizontal $35.0\,\mathrm N$ force acts through its centre and moves it $1.20\,\mathrm m$ from rest. The force is removed and the box slides to rest.

In a second experiment the box rests upright on its $0.40\,\mathrm m$ wide base. A slowly increasing horizontal force is applied at height $0.80\,\mathrm m$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum static friction and explain why motion begins in the first experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the speed when the force is removed and the further distance before the box stops.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine whether the upright box slides or tips first, and calculate the corresponding applied-force threshold.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: For the upright box, determine the application height at which sliding and tipping thresholds coincide.

steps.text: The applied $35.0\,\mathrm N$ exceeds this threshold, so static friction cannot maintain equilibrium; the centre-height force does not overturn the wide box first.
At incipient tipping about the downstream lower corner, $F(0.80)=mg(0.20)$.
This is less than the sliding threshold $29.43\,\mathrm N$, so the upright box tips first. Static friction at this force is below its limiting value.
$H=0.20/0.50=0.400\,\mathrm m$. A lower push produces sliding first; a higher push produces tipping first.

questions.answerSummary: (a) The applied $35.0\,\mathrm N$ exceeds this threshold, so static friction cannot maintain equilibrium; the centre-height force does not overturn the wide box first.; (b) After release, $F_kd=\tfrac12mv^2$, giving $d=1.17853\,\mathrm m\approx1.18\,\mathrm m$.; (c) This is less than the sliding threshold $29.43\,\mathrm N$, so the upright box tips first. Static friction at this force is below its limiting value.; (d) $H=0.20/0.50=0.400\,\mathrm m$. A lower push produces sliding first; a higher push produces tipping first.

questions.title: A moving optical relay and separated emissions
questions.subtopic: A moving optical relay and separated emissions
questions.stem:
Two laboratory beacons lie at $x=0$ and $x=900\,\mathrm m$. The left beacon emits event $A$ at $t=0$; the right emits event $B$ at $t=1.50\,\mathrm{\mu s}$. A relay moves along $+x$ at $0.600c$, passing $x=0$ at $A$. Laboratory and relay clocks are zero at $A$. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The diagram shows the relay worldline (solid) and the left-going light pulse emitted at $B$ (dashed). In the relay frame use $\Delta x\prime=\gamma(\Delta x-v\Delta t)$ and $\Delta t\prime=\gamma(\Delta t-v\Delta x/c^2)$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate $\Delta x\prime$ and $\Delta t\prime$ between emissions $A$ and $B$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the order of the emissions in the relay frame and whether either emission could cause the other.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Keeping the beacon positions fixed, determine the laboratory time of $B$ that would make the two emissions simultaneous in the relay frame.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: For the original emission times, determine the relay-clock reading when it receives the pulse from the right beacon.

steps.text: Because $\Delta t\prime<0$, the relay assigns $B$ before $A$.
The interval is spacelike: $(c\Delta t)^2-(\Delta x)^2=450^2-900^2<0$. No light or slower signal can connect the two emissions, so reversing their coordinate order violates no causality.
The relay has $x=0.600ct$ and the incoming pulse has $x=900-c(t-1.50\times10^{-6})$.
Equating gives $t=2.8125\,\mathrm{\mu s}$ and $x=506.25\,\mathrm m$ in the laboratory.
The relay proper time from $A$ is $t/\gamma=2.25\,\mathrm{\mu s}$.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $\Delta t\prime=1.25(1.50-1.80)=-0.375\,\mathrm{\mu s}$.; (b) The interval is spacelike: $(c\Delta t)^2-(\Delta x)^2=450^2-900^2<0$. No light or slower signal can connect the two emissions, so reversing their coordinate order violates no causality.; (c) $t_B=0.600(900)/c=1.80\,\mathrm{\mu s}$ after $A$ in the laboratory.; (d) The relay proper time from $A$ is $t/\gamma=2.25\,\mathrm{\mu s}$.

questions.title: A rectangular heat-engine cycle
questions.stem: A closed sample of monatomic ideal gas follows $A\to B\to C\to D\to A$ on the diagram, quasi-statically along each straight segment. It takes in heat from a $1000\,\mathrm K$ reservoir during $AB$ and $BC$, and rejects heat to a $100\,\mathrm K$ reservoir during $CD$ and $DA$. Its amount is $0.200\,\mathrm{mol}$ and $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Use $U=3pV/2$ and the convention $Q=\Delta U+W$, with $W$ positive for work by the gas.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the net work by the gas in one cycle and relate its sign to the cycle direction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total heat absorbed from the hot reservoir in one cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the efficiency and compare it with the Carnot limit for the stated reservoirs.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the total entropy change of the gas plus both reservoirs in one cycle. Explain the physical meaning of its sign.

steps.text: The clockwise cycle encloses $\Delta p\Delta V=(2.00\times10^5)(3.00\times10^{-3})$.
$W_{cycle}=+600\,\mathrm J$; expansion at high pressure does more work than compression at low pressure.
The Carnot bound is $1-100/1000=0.900$, so the calculated efficiency is below it.
The gas returns to its initial state, so $\Delta S_{gas}=0$. Rejected heat is $Q_{out}=2850-600=2250\,\mathrm J$.

The positive total entropy change is consistent with an irreversible cycle, including heat transfer across finite temperature differences. Quasi-static gas motion alone does not make the whole process reversible.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $W_{cycle}=+600\,\mathrm J$; expansion at high pressure does more work than compression at low pressure.; (b) $Q_{in}=2850\,\mathrm J$.; (c) The Carnot bound is $1-100/1000=0.900$, so the calculated efficiency is below it.; (d) The positive total entropy change is consistent with an irreversible cycle, including heat transfer across finite temperature differences. Quasi-static gas motion alone does not make the whole process reversible.

questions.title: A moving receiver compares two sound beacons
questions.subtopic: A moving receiver compares two sound beacons
questions.stem:
Two stationary sound beacons $A$ and $B$ lie to the left and right of a moving receiver. The air is stationary. The graph is a spatial snapshot of the wave from $A$, whose period is $2.00\,\mathrm{ms}$. Beacon $B$ emits at $650\,\mathrm{Hz}$. While the receiver moves directly right, its measured frequency ratio is $f_B\prime/f_A\prime=1.80$. The receiver speed is constant and smaller than the sound speed.

The beacons also transmit an optical line of laboratory wavelength $656.0\,\mathrm{nm}$. The receiver spectrometer resolves wavelength differences no smaller than $0.010\,\mathrm{nm}$. Use $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for light.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the graph and period to determine the sound speed and beacon $A$ frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the receiver speed from the measured sound-frequency ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the two sound frequencies actually received.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Estimate the magnitude of the optical wavelength shift caused by this receiver motion. Decide whether the spectrometer can resolve it and explain why the sound shift is much more noticeable.

steps.text: The receiver recedes from $A$ and approaches $B$, so $f_A\prime=500(v-u)/v$ and $f_B\prime=650(v+u)/v$.
The dimensionless motion is $u/v\approx0.161$ for sound but only $u/c\approx1.77\times10^{-7}$ for light; the same speed gives very different fractional shifts.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $f_A=1/T=500\,\mathrm{Hz}$.; (b) $u=53.2258\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx53.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to the right.; (c) $f_B\prime=754.839\,\mathrm{Hz}\approx755\,\mathrm{Hz}$, retaining the ratio $1.80$.; (d) The dimensionless motion is $u/v\approx0.161$ for sound but only $u/c\approx1.77\times10^{-7}$ for light; the same speed gives very different fractional shifts.

questions.title: Recoil energy and a nuclear-scale scattering test
questions.subtopic: Recoil energy and a nuclear-scale scattering test
questions.stem:
An initially stationary $^{212}_{84}\mathrm{Po}$ nucleus emits an alpha particle and becomes a lead nucleus. The decay releases $8.95\,\mathrm{MeV}$ of kinetic energy. For recoil calculations take the daughter-to-alpha mass ratio as $208:4$ and use nonrelativistic mechanics.

An alpha particle from this decay is subsequently directed head-on towards a stationary $^{118}_{50}\mathrm{Sn}$ nucleus. For this scattering calculation neglect the tin recoil and use electrostatic repulsion until nuclear-scale distances are reached. Use $k=8.99\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ and $R=1.20\times10^{-15}A^{1/3}\,\mathrm m$.

parts.prompt: Write the nuclear decay equation and state the momentum relationship between the products.

parts.prompt: Determine the kinetic energies of the alpha particle and lead nucleus.

parts.label: c

steps.text: The momenta are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction because the parent initially has zero momentum.
The energies sum to $8.95\,\mathrm{MeV}$, so $K_\alpha=8.95(208/212)$ and $K_{Pb}=8.95(4/212)$.

This extrapolation reaches the finite-sized nucleus, where the point-charge/electrostatic-only approximation can fail and nuclear interactions become relevant; it is a scale estimate, not a guaranteed scattering prediction.

questions.answerSummary: (a) The momenta are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction because the parent initially has zero momentum.; (b) $K_\alpha=8.78113\,\mathrm{MeV}\approx8.78\,\mathrm{MeV}$ and $K_{Pb}=0.168868\,\mathrm{MeV}\approx0.169\,\mathrm{MeV}$.; (c) $r_{min}=1.63806\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm m\approx1.64\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm m$.; (d) This extrapolation reaches the finite-sized nucleus, where the point-charge/electrostatic-only approximation can fail and nuclear interactions become relevant; it is a scale estimate, not a guaranteed scattering prediction.

questions.title: A reciprocal-wavelength photoelectric fit
questions.stem:
A vacuum photocell is illuminated by monochromatic light. A model experimental fit over its emitting range is
$$V_s=(1.240\,\mathrm V)X-2.600\,\mathrm V,\qquad X=\frac{1/\lambda}{10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}}.$$
The plotted $V_s$ is the magnitude of the stopping potential. Use $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. In part(d) use accepted values $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Assume independent single-photon emission and no space-charge limitation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the fit and the photoelectric equation to determine the experimental Planck constant and the metal work function in electronvolts.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the threshold wavelength predicted by the fit.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At $300\,\mathrm{nm}$ the optical power is increased by a factor4 without changing wavelength. Predict the saturation-current and stopping-potential changes, with reasons.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Determine the de Broglie wavelength of the most energetic electrons emitted under $300\,\mathrm{nm}$ illumination.

steps.text: From $eV_s=hc/\lambda-\Phi$ and $1/\lambda=10^6X$, the fitted slope is $10^6hc/e$.
The intercept gives $\Phi/e=2.600\,\mathrm V$, hence work function $2.600\,\mathrm{eV}$.
At fixed wavelength, four times the power means four times the photon arrival rate and therefore four times the saturation current under the assumptions.
The photon energy and work function are unchanged, so the maximum electron kinetic energy and stopping potential are unchanged.
The fit at $X=1/(300\times10^{-9}\times10^6)=3.33333$ gives $V_s=1.53333\,\mathrm V$ and $K_{max}=eV_s$.

questions.answerSummary: (a) The intercept gives $\Phi/e=2.600\,\mathrm V$, hence work function $2.600\,\mathrm{eV}$.; (b) $\lambda_0=1/(10^6X_0)=4.76923\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m\approx477\,\mathrm{nm}$.; (c) The photon energy and work function are unchanged, so the maximum electron kinetic energy and stopping potential are unchanged.; (d) $\lambda_{dB}\approx9.92\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m=0.992\,\mathrm{nm}$, using unrounded values.

questions.title: A floating cylinder as a tunable oscillator
questions.subtopic: A floating cylinder as a tunable oscillator
questions.stem:
A uniform vertical cylinder has mass $0.900\,\mathrm{kg}$, height $0.300\,\mathrm m$ and constant cross-sectional area $6.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. A frictionless vertical guide prevents tipping without exerting a vertical force. It floats in water of density $1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Use $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. For this model ignore damping, surface tension and the inertia of the surrounding water. Displacements remain small enough that the cylinder is neither fully submerged nor lifted clear of the water. Take downward displacement from equilibrium as $x$.

The cylinder is released from rest at amplitude $0.0400\,\mathrm m$. A later run adds a $0.300\,\mathrm{kg}$ payload fixed rigidly to its top and repeats the same displacement from the new equilibrium.

parts.label: d

steps.text: A downward displacement adds buoyancy $\rho gAx$, so $F_{net}=-\rho gAx$ and $a=-(\rho gA/m)x$.
The total oscillating mass is $1.200\,\mathrm{kg}$ while $\rho gA$ is unchanged, so $T_{loaded}=2\pi\sqrt{1.200/58.86}$.

The new draft is $1.200/(1000\times0.00600)=0.200\,\mathrm m$. During oscillation it ranges from $0.160$ to $0.240\,\mathrm m$, strictly between $0$ and the $0.300\,\mathrm m$ height, so the stated model remains geometrically valid.

During oscillation it ranges from $0.160$ to $0.240\,\mathrm m$, strictly between $0$ and the $0.300\,\mathrm m$ height, so the stated model remains geometrically valid.

parts.prompt: Determine the rod acceleration at this speed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the terminal speed and the steady electrical power dissipated. Explain the corresponding mechanical energy balance.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In a separate run with a constant field of $0.800\,\mathrm T$, determine the acceleration when speed is $2.00\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the new terminal speed. Other parameters are unchanged.

steps.text: Positive charges are driven upward along the moving rod; the induced current is upward through the rod, giving a leftward magnetic force.
$F_B=BIL=0.0500\,\mathrm N$ left, opposing the rightward pull.
At terminal speed kinetic energy is constant; all pulling power is converted to resistor heating through electromagnetic induction.
The terminal speed is $0.500\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, one quarter of the original because magnetic drag is proportional to $B^2v$.

questions.title: A luminous star from its spectrum and flux
questions.subtopic: A luminous star from its spectrum and flux
questions.stem:
A star at distance $12.0\,\mathrm{pc}$ has apparent brightness $1.20\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Its continuum spectrum has the maximum shown. Model it as a spherical black body. Use $1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.086\times10^{16}\,\mathrm m$, Wien constant $2.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$, $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$ and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Suppose its luminosity is sustained by hydrogen fusion in which $0.700\%$ of the processed hydrogen rest mass is converted to released energy. For comparison, the Sun has radius $6.96\times10^8\,\mathrm m$ and effective temperature approximately $5800\,\mathrm K$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the effective temperature and luminosity of the star.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate its radius.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the rate at which hydrogen mass must be processed, distinguishing it from the rate of rest-mass conversion to energy.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Compare the star with the Sun on an HR diagram and explain the physical balance that permits a stable stellar radius. State one limit of inferring an exact evolutionary stage from the supplied observations.

steps.text: $L=4\pi d^2b\approx2.07\times10^{28}\,\mathrm W$, converting $12.0\,\mathrm{pc}$ to metres before squaring.
The rate of mass actually converted to energy is $L/c^2\approx2.30\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.
Only a fraction $0.00700$ of the processed hydrogen is converted, so $\dot m_H=L/(0.00700c^2)$.

The star is slightly hotter and far more luminous than the Sun, placing it above and slightly left of the Sun on a conventional HR diagram; its much larger radius is consistent with an evolved enlarged star rather than a Sun-sized object.
In a stable star, inward gravitational pressure is balanced by outward thermal pressure and/or radiation pressure, with fusion providing the energy supply.

A precise evolutionary stage is not fixed by temperature and luminosity alone: stellar mass, composition, age or additional spectroscopic/evolutionary evidence is needed. Accept a physically justified equivalent limitation.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $L=4\pi d^2b\approx2.07\times10^{28}\,\mathrm W$, converting $12.0\,\mathrm{pc}$ to metres before squaring.; (b) $R\approx4.67\times10^9\,\mathrm m$, about $6.7$ solar radii.; (c) $\dot m_H\approx3.28\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$, rather than $L/c^2$.; (d) A precise evolutionary stage is not fixed by temperature and luminosity alone: stellar mass, composition, age or additional spectroscopic/evolutionary evidence is needed. Accept a physically justified equivalent limitation.
